$schema_note: #353: why each upstream tool is NOT in the interop profile. The mechanical half — which upstream tools we ported and pruned versus never ported — is COMPUTED by scripts/validate-tools.sh from the two trees. This file records only the JUDGEMENT: why the fork does not advertise it. Keep no counts here; a count in this file would be a second source of truth for something a command already prints, and every prose count in this repo has gone stale (#359).

categories.unsafe-here: The capability lets an agent damage an instance or reach past what this fork is for, and no interop task needs it. Excluded on purpose; not a candidate.
categories.not-interop: A legitimate upstream capability outside this fork's interoperability remit — instance administration, the server registry, the skill/KB machinery, agent telemetry. Excluded on scope, not on merit.
categories.covered-here: This fork already answers the same question through a tool it does advertise. Adopting it would give a caller two ways to ask one thing.
categories.wanted: Would help interop work and is not excluded on principle — only not adopted yet. `tracking` names where the decision is being made.

global_kill.why: Deletes an entire global. Interop message headers, bodies and queues live in globals, so a wrong argument destroys a production's history with nothing to roll back to.

global_preview.why: Its purpose is to mint the confirm_token global_kill requires; without that tool it authorises nothing. Excluded with the capability it belongs to rather than left as a half.

iris_global.why: Writes and kills global nodes directly, underneath the class layer that maintains interop indices and search tables. A write that looks correct at the global level can leave a production's own structures inconsistent.

iris_ws_exec.why: Arbitrary ObjectScript in a terminal session whose variables persist across calls, so what a call does depends on calls before it. This fork deliberately routes ObjectScript through iris_execute's disposable scratch class, where each call is self-contained and its failure is attributable.

iris_ws_open.why: Opens the persistent terminal session iris_ws_exec runs in. Excluded with the capability rather than leaving its lifecycle half-advertised.

iris_ws_close.why: Closes the persistent terminal session. Excluded with the capability it belongs to.

iris_admin.why: Instance administration dispatcher — users, roles, databases, webapps, locks, processes. Interop work needs none of it, and its write actions reach far outside a production.

iris_namespace_create.why: Creates a namespace and its database. Provisioning an instance is a step before interop development, done deliberately by a person.

iris_database_list.why: Database directories, mount state and sizes: instance capacity, not production behaviour.

iris_database_stats.why: Database disk usage. Same axis as iris_database_list — storage administration.

iris_mirror_status.why: Mirror membership and role. High availability is an instance property; a production behaves the same on either member.

iris_system_performance.why: SystemPerformance (pbuttons) profiles and runs — whole-instance performance profiling, read by a person diagnosing the platform rather than the integration.

query_audit_log.why: Reads %SYS.Audit. Security auditing of the instance, and the answers are about who did what to IRIS, not about what a production did with a message.

journal_search.why: Journal SetKill records. A recovery and forensics instrument for the database, not a view of a production's message flow — iris_interop_query answers that.

iris_servers.why: Lists the multi-server connection pool. This fork connects to one instance at a time, named by IRIS_HOST/IRIS_NAMESPACE, and check_config reports which.

iris_add_server.why: Registers a server in the connection pool. Nothing in the fork's one-instance model reads that registry.

iris_remove_server.why: Removes a registered server. Excluded with the registry it edits.

iris_import_servers.why: Imports server definitions from VS Code / Cursor settings into the pool config. Excluded with the registry it populates.

iris_test_server.why: Probes a REGISTERED server for reachability. The fork's equivalent question — is the configured instance answering — is what check_config and the IRIS_UNREACHABLE envelope already report.

iris_reload_pool.why: Hot-reloads the multi-server pool from disk. There is no pool to reload in a one-instance connection.

iris_containers.why: Container lifecycle — list, select, start. Provisioning the instance is a step before the work; the fork talks to whatever is already listening.

iris_list_containers.why: Enumerates running IRIS Docker containers. Same axis as iris_containers, which already dispatches it upstream.

iris_select_container.why: Switches the active connection to a container mid-session. A connection that changes underneath a sequence of calls makes every earlier result ambiguous about which instance it came from.

iris_start_sandbox.why: Starts a project container via the iris-devtester CLI. Environment provisioning, and it depends on a CLI the fork does not require.

capability_matrix.why: Roles assigned to an arbitrary user. Administering other people's access is outside the remit; my_access answers the question a blocked caller actually has.

iris_generate.why: Builds a prompt plus namespace context for a model to generate a class. This fork's skills own how interop classes are written, including the naming and TDD rules a generic generator does not know.

iris_generate_class.why: Generates a class through an external LLM (needs IRIS_GENERATE_CLASS_MODEL and OPENAI_API_KEY). A second model inside the toolchain, with its own key and its own conventions.

agent_history.why: Recent tool calls of the running session — introspection of the agent, not of IRIS.

agent_info.why: Session and learning-agent statistics. Same axis as agent_history.

agent_stats.why: Skill, pattern and KB counts of the learning agent. Same axis as agent_history.

telemetry_query.why: Queries the durable tool-call telemetry record. Useful for studying how an agent behaves; it answers nothing about a production.

telemetry_export_trace.why: Exports dispatch-trace records of tool calls. Same axis as telemetry_query.

kb.why: Knowledge-base index and recall over ^KBCHUNKS. This fork delivers guidance as skills that load into the session, not as a retrieval store.

kb_index.why: Indexes markdown into the knowledge base. Excluded with the KB machinery.

kb_recall.why: Searches the knowledge base. Excluded with the KB machinery.

skill.why: Manages the learning-agent skill registry in ^SKILLS. The fork's skills are files in the plugin, versioned and reviewed, not rows an agent writes at runtime.

skill_list.why: Lists registry and bundled skills. Excluded with the registry.

skill_describe.why: Describes one registry skill. Excluded with the registry.

skill_search.why: Searches registry skills. Excluded with the registry.

skill_forget.why: Deletes a skill from the registry. Excluded with the registry.

skill_propose.why: Mines recorded tool calls to synthesise new skills. The fork's skills are authored and reviewed, so a synthesised one would enter unreviewed.

skill_optimize.why: Optimises a skill with DSPy (needs OBJECTSCRIPT_DSPY). Excluded with the registry, and it adds a dependency the fork does not carry.

skill_share.why: Opens a GitHub PR to publish a skill. A tool that pushes to a remote on an agent's behalf is outside what an interop session should be able to do.

skill_community.why: Browses and installs skills from subscribed GitHub repos into ^SKILLS. Excluded with the registry, and it installs unreviewed content.

skill_community_list.why: Lists skills from subscribed community packages. Excluded with the community registry.

skill_community_install.why: Installs a community skill into the local registry. Excluded with the community registry.

mermaid_class.why: A superclass-chain diagram for any class. The structural question an interop reviewer asks is the production's topology, which mermaid_production answers and #352 is evaluating.

iris_source_control.why: SCM status, menu, checkout. iris_doc does the checkout itself on every write — including the elicitation dialog when IRIS asks for confirmation — so the caller never has to sequence it.

debug_source_map.why: Builds a .INT source map for a class. iris_debug is the fork's dispatcher for this, and an abort from iris_execute is already enriched with the .CLS line before it reaches the caller.

debug_map_int_to_cls.why: Maps a .INT offset back to a .CLS line. Reached through iris_debug here, and applied automatically to a runtime abort.

debug_get_error_logs.why: Recent IRIS error-log entries. iris_get_log reads the logs this fork's callers need, and iris_interop_query(what=logs) reads the production's own.

debug_capture_packet.why: Captures error state plus recent log entries as one bundle. Its two halves are what iris_debug and iris_get_log already return.

compare_namespace.why: Diffs all classes across two namespaces. The drift report a reviewer writes by hand today, and the fork's own conformance pass needs exactly this answer.

compare_document.why: Diffs one document across two servers. The per-class half of the same drift question, and the direct check for 'the file on disk and the class in IRIS have diverged'.

stream_inspect.why: Reads a stream body by OID. Interop message bodies are streams, so this is a first-class interop read; measured here that a fresh %OpenId reads from the start, so it does not consume what it inspects.

iris_generate_test.why: Generates a %UnitTest.TestCase for an existing class, introspecting it first. The fork's own workflow is test-first, so the shape is right even though it needs an external model key.

mermaid_production.why: A flowchart of a production's configured items. The topology is what a reviewer reads first, and nothing advertised here renders it.

resolve_storage.why: Returns a class's global maps from %Dictionary.CompiledStorage. Reading a storage definition is the safe half of the area this fork refuses to edit, and it answers where a persistent message body actually lives.

resolve_dynamic_dispatch.why: Finds every compiled class implementing a method, for $classmethod(var, method). Routing and business-rule code dispatches dynamically, which is where a static read of the source stops being enough.

iris_search.why: Full-text search across documents via Atelier. The question 'which class references this' has no other answer in the profile; iris_symbols searches names, not bodies.

iris_info.why: Read-only namespace discovery — documents, recently modified, namespace config, IRIS version. what=modified answers 'what did I just change', which nothing advertised here does.

iris_namespace_list.why: Lists namespaces, read-only. The fork's commonest configuration failure is targeting a namespace that does not exist, and the refusal for it can name the namespaces that do only if something can enumerate them.

my_access.why: The current user's roles. The IRIS_FORBIDDEN hint in this fork tells the caller to go and read their roles in the Management Portal; this answers that in-tool, on the payload that raised the question.
